practice.foundation[4]: The diagram title states a 100 m race, but the supplied graph represents only 96 m: $16+48+16=96$. Remove or correct the inconsistent distance label; the acceleration calculation is correct.

practice.foundation[5]: Development 3(b–c), lines 2033–2041, asks for each animal's acceleration separately, but never asks which accelerates faster. Retain the supported calculations and remove the unsupported comparison demand; update the structure slug to describe the retained task.

practice.foundation[6]: The booklet asks students to calculate deceleration, but never to compare two deceleration rates. Remove the unsupported comparison demand and make the structure slug describe calculating deceleration.
practice.development[1]: The structure slug 'deceleration-to-rest' contradicts the final speed of 15 m/s. Change it to describe deceleration between nonzero speeds.

practice.development[3]: Comparing rates and calculating their difference from one graph and one verbal description is not asked in the booklet. Replace with a supported graph-based acceleration calculation of the same tier. Runner B is also not stated to accelerate at a constant rate, so its constant acceleration cannot be inferred.

practice.development[5]: Guided Practice (a–c), lines 1929–1943, supports calculating all three stage accelerations, but does not ask students to classify every stage. Remove the unsupported classification demand and update the structure slug; the calculations are correct.

practice.mastery[1]: The booklet asks for individual acceleration and deceleration rates, but never their difference. Replace the unsupported difference task with a supported graph-stage rate calculation of the same tier and update the structure slug.

quiz.q1: Option 1's explanation says one gridline below 15, which is 14 on this graph and gives 2.8, not 2.4. Correct that value or explanation. Option 2 rounds $1/3$ to 0.33 without a stated rounding convention; use an exact value or state the rounding.
quiz.q2: Option 2 rounds $1/3$ to 0.33 without a stated rounding convention; use an exact value or state the rounding.

quiz.q4: The source explains zero acceleration over a given interval and asks for its numerical value, but never asks students to identify the interval. Replace this with a supported zero-acceleration calculation or explanation under the same quiz id and update the structure slug.

quiz.q5: Option 1's explanation is inaccurate: the total journey's speed change is zero, so dividing that change by 13 gives zero, not 1.23. Name the actual mistake of dividing the final-stage speed decrease by the whole journey time. State the rounding convention for options 1 and 2, or use exact values.

quiz.q6: The booklet never asks students to compare decelerations or calculate their difference. Replace with a supported graph-based deceleration question under the same id and update the structure slug.
quiz.q7: Options 1 and 2 use rounding to one decimal place without stating that convention. State the rounding or use exact values.

quiz.q8: The booklet never asks for the difference between acceleration and deceleration magnitudes. Replace with a supported graph-stage rate calculation under the same id and update the structure slug. The current final distractor also rounds without a stated convention.

theory: Qualify the steepness statement: compare gradients using the axis scales, and describe greater steepness as a greater acceleration or deceleration magnitude. A visually steeper line on a differently scaled graph need not represent a greater rate.
summary: Removed unsupported comparison and classification demands, replaced unsupported tasks with cited graph-rate calculations, corrected the race label and structure slugs, and repaired quiz explanations and rounding instructions. Qualified the theory's steepness statement using axis scales; all original item locators remain, so no whole items were removed.
reviewSummary: All fourteen requested items have correct answers, assess booklet question types and stay within the target skill; each reviewed quiz has exactly one correct option and consistent distractor explanations. The theory agrees with the booklet's gradient method, and no repairs or removals are required.
